'''Gregory B. Jaczko''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|j|ɑː|s|k|oʊ}};{{citation needed|date=August 2017}} born October&nbsp;29, 1970, [[Norristown, Pennsylvania]]) is a physicist who is the 13th and former chairman of the [[Nuclear Regulatory Commission|U.S.&nbsp;Nuclear Regulatory Commission]] (NRC) from 2009 to 2012.<ref name="fire">[https://www.nytimes.com/2012/05/22/us/gregory-jaczko-to-resign-as-nrc-chairman-after-stormy-tenure.html "N.R.C. Chairman to Resign After Stormy Tenure"], ''[[New York Times]]'', May 22, 2012, retrieved May 21, 2012</ref><ref name="macfarlane">[https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/organization/commission/macfarlane.html Macfarlane], NRC website.</ref> While at the NRC, he voted against the opening of new nuclear plants; an inspector general report found that he sought unilaterally and improperly to block the [[Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository]] project from advancing. After leaving the NRC, Jaczko called for a global ban on nuclear power.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2019|title=Why the man once in charge of U.S. nuclear energy now wants to see it banned|work=CBC|url=https://www.cbc.ca/radio/asithappens/as-it-happens-friday-edition-1.5140405/why-the-man-once-in-charge-of-u-s-nuclear-energy-now-wants-to-see-it-banned-1.5140429}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Jaczko was raised in [[Albany, New York]],<ref name=allgov /> the son of Kathryn Marie and Bela L. Jaczko.<ref>{{Cite news|first= |last= |authorlink=   |title=Obituary: Kathryn M. Jaczko   |newspaper=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date= January 31, 2014|url= https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/baltimoresun/name/kathryn-jaczko-obituary?id=6981722 |accessdate=}}</ref> He studied physics and philosophy at [[Cornell University]] in [[Ithaca, New York]]; he earned a bachelor in the two disciplines there in 1993.<ref name=allgov /> In 1999, he earned a doctorate in [[Particle physics|theoretical particle physics]] from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name=allgov />

He is married to journalist [[Leigh Ann Caldwell]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://leighanncaldwell.com/home/About_Me.html|title=Leigh Ann Caldwell - A Little More|work=leighanncaldwell.com|access-date=2012-09-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121113210623/http://leighanncaldwell.com/home/About_Me.html|archive-date=2012-11-13|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Political career==
Jaczko served as a Congressional Science Fellow in the office of U.S.&nbsp;Representative [[Ed Markey]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], on the basis of an [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] ''Science and Technology Policy Fellowship''. He also worked as an adjunct professor for Physics and Public Policy<ref name=aps>Meghan Anzelc: [http://www.aps.org/units/fgsa/careers/non-traditional/jaczko.cfm Gregory Jaczko, Ph.D. Physics, Commissioner, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission]. ''[[American Physical Society]]'' / www.aps.org</ref> under Dr. Francis Slakey<ref name=slakey>[http://spi.georgetown.edu/slakey.html Dr. Francis Slakey] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719201743/http://spi.georgetown.edu/slakey.html |date=2011-07-19 }}. ''[[Georgetown University]]'' / spi.georgetown.edu</ref> at [[Georgetown University]] in Washington,&nbsp;D.C.<ref name=nrc>[https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/organization/commission/jaczko.html Chairman Gregory B. Jaczko]. ''[[Nuclear Regulatory Commission]] / Nrc.gov'', retrieved March 16, 2011</ref>

He later advised the [[United States Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works]] on issues regarding [[nuclear power]].<ref name=allgov /> He served as appropriations director for U.S.&nbsp;Senator [[Harry Reid]] and as Reid's science policy advisor.<ref name=nrc />

[[File:Harry Reid swears in Gregory Jaczko 4-28-08.jpg|thumb|left|Senator [[Harry Reid]] swearing in Jaczko]]

===Nuclear Regulatory Commission===
Jaczko was first sworn in as a Commissioner of the [[Nuclear Regulatory Commission]] (NRC) on January 21, 2005. On May 13, 2009, President [[Barack Obama|Obama]] designated him the organization's chairman,<ref name=allgov>[http://www.allgov.com/Official/Jaczko_Gregory Name: Jaczko, Gregory; Current position: Chairman], . ''Allgov.com'', retrieved March 16, 2011.</ref> its principal executive officer and official spokesperson.<ref name=nrc /><ref name=Commission>{{cite web|url=https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/organization/commission/former-commissioners/klein.html|title=Commissioner Dale E. Klein|date=2012-03-29|accessdate=2012-10-13}}</ref> The chairman is responsible for long-range planning as well as budgetary and certain personnel functions of the NRC. “He also has authority for all NRC functions pertaining to a potential emergency involving an NRC licensee”.<ref name=nrc />

=== Policy positions ===
Jaczko has asserted that the greatest possible openness furthers the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's work on the protection of the environment and of public health and safety.<ref name=nrc /> He encourages “licensees, vendors, state and local governments, interest groups, and the general public” to participate in the commission's policy-making efforts.<ref name=nrc /> Efforts by Jaczko to strengthen security regulations for [[nuclear power plant]]s have included requiring new such plants to be able to withstand an aircraft crash.<ref name=nrc />

On February 9, 2012, Jaczko cast the lone dissenting vote on plans to build the first new nuclear power plant in more than 30 years when the NRC voted 4–1 to allow Atlanta-based Southern Co to build and operate two new nuclear power reactors at its existing [[Vogtle Electric Generating Plant|Vogtle nuclear power plant]] in Georgia. He cited safety concerns stemming from Japan's 2011 [[Fukushima nuclear disaster]], saying "I cannot support issuing this license as if Fukushima never happened".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-nuclear-nrc-idUSTRE8182J720120209  |title=U.S. approves first new nuclear plant in a generation  |author=Ayesha Rascoe | date=Feb 9, 2012  |work=Reuters }}</ref>

=== Management style and resignation ===
A report by Nuclear Regulatory Commission Inspector General Hubert&nbsp;T. Bell found that Jaczko "strategically" withheld information from his colleagues in an effort to keep plans for the [[Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository]] from advancing.<ref name="wsjlink">{{cite news|author = The Wall Street Journal
 |url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702304259304576375961521636474
 |title = Report Slams U.S. Nuclear Regulator
 |publisher= [[The Wall Street Journal]]
 |date = 2011-06-10
 |accessdate = 2011-06-10}}</ref><ref name="bloomlink">{{cite news|author = Bloomberg News
 |url = https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2011-06-10/nrc-chief-withheld-information-on-yucca-plans-watchdog-says-3-.html
 |title = NRC Chief Withheld Information on Yucca Plans, Watchdog Says
 |publisher=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]] |date = 2011-06-10
 |accessdate = 2011-06-10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2011-06-14|title=Gregory Jaczko 'unilaterally' stopped work on US nuclear dump|url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2011/jun/14/gregory-jaczko-nuclear-dump-closed|access-date=2022-02-22|website=[[The Guardian]]|language=en}}</ref>

In October 2011, all the other four NRC commissioners—two Democrats and two Republicans—sent a letter to the White House expressing "grave concern" about Jaczko's actions at the NRC. On December&nbsp;14, 2011, Commissioner William Ostendorff, a Republican, told a House oversight committee that Jaczko's "bullying and intimidation... should not and cannot be tolerated."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/wireStory/nrc-commissioners-chairman-jaczko-bully-15153720#.TujKYlbAQxE|title=U.S. News - National News|author=ABC News|work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]}}</ref>

At a House Government Reform and Oversight Committee hearing on December 14, 2011, NRC Commissioner William Magwood, a fellow Democrat, testified about what he called Jaczko's abusive behavior towards employees, especially female subordinates. “One woman told me that she felt the chairman was actually irritated with someone else, but took it out on her,” Magwood said. “Another said she was angry at herself for being brought to tears in front of male colleagues. A third described how she couldn’t stop shaking after her experience. She sat, talking with her supervisor until she could calm down sufficiently to drive home.”<ref name="The Hill">{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/100345-nuke-commissioners-accuse-chairman-of-abusing-staff-withholding-information/|title=Nuke commissioners accuse chairman of abusing staff, withholding information|work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref>

A report by the Government Reform and Oversight Committee detailed incidents indicating what was cited as Jaczko's "propensity for angry outbursts and aggressive behavior." A 2012 NRC Office of Inspector General report identified multiple examples where his behavior was not supportive of an open and collaborative work environment.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.energybiz.com/article/12/06/nrc-inspector-general-clears-jaczko|title=NRC Inspector General Clears Jaczko|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518104931/http://www.energybiz.com/article/12/06/nrc-inspector-general-clears-jaczko|archive-date=2015-05-18}}</ref> Top House Republicans called on President Obama to dismiss Jaczko.<ref name="The Hill"/>

Jaczko said problems at the agency were not his fault but instead stem from "lack of understanding" on the part of others.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.businessweek.com/ap/financialnews/D9RKDPA00.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130728192756/http://www.businessweek.com/ap/financialnews/D9RKDPA00.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 28, 2013|title=NRC commissioners: Chairman Jaczko is a 'bully'|author=MATTHEW DALY|work=Businessweek.com}}</ref> Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid defended Jaczko, saying his critics are attacking him because "they’re concerned about the nuclear industry. He’s concerned about the American people."<ref>[https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2011-12-14/nrc-chief-s-temper-undermining-agency-house-republicans-say.html "NRC Chief’s Temper Undermining Agency, House Republicans Say"], ''Bloomberg'', 14 December 2011</ref>

[[Peter A. Bradford]], who was a commission member from 1977 to 1982, has also defended Jaczko. Bradford said it was not unusual for the commissioners to disagree strongly, and added that he did not believe that "the chairman is somehow raging around the agency and intimidating the staff".<ref name="bradford"/> He also argued that, although the letter about Jaczko was written by two Republicans and two Democrats, it was necessarily bi-partisan in the context of nuclear politics. He claimed that "In Washington, you’ve got a situation where the ‘nuclear party’ transcends the Republican and Democratic party," adding that "You’ve got four members of the nuclear party writing a letter about the chairman, who’s never been a member of the nuclear party."<ref name="bradford">{{cite web |url=http://green.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/12/28/in-agency-smackdown-a-critique-of-the-nuclear-party/ |title=Agency Smackdown, Round 2: A Critique of 'the Nuclear Party' |author=Matthew Wald |date=December 28, 2011 |work=[[The New York Times]] }}</ref>

On May 21, 2012, he announced his resignation pending the confirmation of the next person to fill this role.<ref name= fire /> On July 9, 2012, Jaczko was replaced by [[Allison Macfarlane]], a nuclear waste expert and associate professor at George Mason University.<ref  name="macfarlane" />

In 2013 he was appointed by Harry Reid to a post on a Congressional panel overseeing the [[National Nuclear Security Administration]]<ref>Niels Lesniewski "[https://rollcall.com/2013/04/23/reid-finds-ex-aide-jaczko-a-new-gig/ Reid Finds Ex-Aide Jaczko a New Gig]", ''Roll Call'',  April 23, 2013. Retrieved Jan 29, 2022.</ref>

===2026 congressional campaign===
Jaczko ran for the Democratic nomination for the [[District of Columbia]]'s [[Non-voting members of the United States House of Representatives|non-voting delegate]], vying to succeed [[Eleanor Holmes Norton]], in the [[2026 United States House of Representatives election in the District of Columbia|2026 election]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Payne |first1=Sarah |title=Who is Running for Nomination as DC Delegate in the Democratic Primary?|url=https://www.hillrag.com/2026/04/30/who-is-running-for-nomination-as-dc-delegate-in-the-democratic-primary/ |website=HillRag |date=30 April 2026}}</ref> By May, he had raised $113,000 and ''[[Politico (magazine)|Politico]]'' described his bid as a "long-shot" compared to [[District of Columbia Council|council]]members [[Robert White (Washington, D.C., politician)|Robert White]] and [[Brooke Pinto]]. His stated campaign goals included boosting the federal workforce, improving federal agencies' work with city residents and government, exempting the city from federal income taxes, and electricity affordability through renewable energy build-out.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eenews.net/articles/ex-nuclear-regulator-wages-long-shot-bid-for-congress/|title=Ex-nuclear regulator wages long-shot bid for Congress|date=June 15, 2026|website=[[Politico (magazine)|Politico]]|first=Timothy|last=Cama}}</ref> He placed 5th in the June primary election with 2.88% of the vote.<ref name=DCBoE>{{cite news |title=Primary and Special Election 2026 - Election Night Unofficial Results |website=District of Columbia Board of Elections |date=June 16, 2026 |access-date=June 17, 2026 |url=https://electionresults.dcboe.org/election_results/2026-Primary-Election}}</ref>

== In media ==
Gregory Jaczko has an important cameo appearance in the 2023 documentary film ''[[SOS: The San Onofre Syndrome]]'', directed by James Heddle, Mary Beth Brangan and Morgan Peterson. In a recent interview<ref>{{Cite web |last=HaLevy |first=Libbe |date=September 26, 2023 |title="SOS – San Onofre Syndrome" Film is a Knockout! Directors Mary Beth Brangan & Jim Heddle |url=https://nuclearhotseat.com/podcast/nh-640-sos-san-onofre-syndrome-film-a-knockout-directors-mary-beth-brangan-jim-heddle/ }}</ref> producer Mary Beth Brangan stated that it was the [[Fukushima nuclear disaster]] that set her and her life partner, James Heddle, into the making of the film. The film documents a special visit prime minister [[Naoto Kan]] made to San Diego on June 4, 2013 in order to participate in a panel entitled "Fukushima: Ongoing Lessons for California",  [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TRTtGNtJ8sQ]<ref>{{Cite news |last=St. John |first=Alison |date=June 4, 2013 |title=Lessons from Fukushima to San Onofre |work=KPBS |url=https://www.kpbs.org/news/environment/2013/06/04/lessons-fukushima }}</ref> along with Nuclear Regulatory Commission chair Gregory Jaczko, former NRC Commissioner [[Peter A. Bradford]], and nuclear engineer [[Arnold Gundersen|Arnie Gundersen]], where they discussed nuclear power's risks.

In the film, which issues a critical warning that America's 55 nuclear power plants, each of which has tons of intensely [[radioactive waste]] that lasts millennia—in inadequate temporary storage containers with no plans to repair them—are putting their local communities and national security at grave risk. In archival footage from a [[KPBS (TV)|KPBS]] news program, Jaczko stated: "But frankly once they get loaded, I don't see them ever taking those canisters out of there. Realistically, they're not going to move them out. So those permits will be extended. The operational period will be extended repeatedly, and you will have a de facto burial site."<ref>{{Cite news |last=St. John |first=Alison |date=June 4, 2013 |title=Lessons from Fukushima for San Onofre |work=KPBS |url=https://www.kpbs.org/news/environment/2013/06/04/lessons-fukushima |access-date=November 8, 2011}}</ref>
